posts.caption:
Same teams as last week? I sat out twice already. Who's keeping track?

Nobody has to. The app makes the rounds: new partners every round, and it tells you who is resting.

By the end it's the same for everyone. Everybody played as often, and everybody sat out as often. No counting, no arguing about it.

Competitive padel with the people you actually like. Free on iOS and Android.

Type in the score. That's it.

After a match you enter the three sets. Your opponent taps to confirm, and the table updates itself. No spreadsheet, no photo of a scorecard in the group chat.

A point for every set you win, so every set counts.

EffePadelle. Free on the App Store and Google Play.

Eight friends booked a house and two courts for a weekend. They came home with a league table.

Three days, three tournaments, one winner a day. You book the courts for an hour and a half and choose how long a round lasts. Twenty minutes gives you six rounds.

Every round the app puts new pairs together and tells everyone which court to walk to. A buzzer calls the switch. The host types in the games each pair won and the table is right straight away.

Swipe for the weekend. You book the courts, the app does the rest.

See who's winning, all season.

Every score goes straight into the table, so the standings are always right and always in your pocket. Tap a name to see someone's profile and every match they've played.

The friendly game was never really that friendly anyway.

EffePadelle. Free on the App Store and Google Play.

Somebody in the group chat did the maths for twelve people and got it wrong twice.

Now you tap add new, pick a suggested tournament and answer two questions: how many of you, and how you want to partner up. Courts, rounds, round length and changeover follow from that. Twelve players becomes three courts and five rounds before you start.

Nobody gets the same partner twice, everyone plays as often, and everyone is on court for about ninety minutes. One tip: book longer than you play.

Swipe for the setup. Pick one, answer two questions, send the link.

Tuesday? Can't. Thursday? I'm out. Next week then?

Forty messages later there's still no evening. So the app asks your calendar instead. It fills in when you can play, morning, afternoon or evening, and checks it for everyone in the group.

Then it finds the evening you're all free. Friday the 20th, four out of four. Planned.

Competitive padel with the people you actually like. Free on iOS and Android.

Same group, same court, every week. Only now it counts.

EffePadelle turns your padel friends into a competition you run yourself. Pick a format, send one link, and everyone's in.

There's a table, there's a winner, and there's finally an answer to who's actually best.

Free to start on the App Store and Google Play.

Your phone is in a bag. Your round changed anyway.

So the tournament is on your wrist now. The timer the host started counts down on every watch at once, and when the round ends it taps you, with your next partner and your court.

Nobody stands still between rounds asking who they're with now. You look down and go.

Swipe to see it. Apple Watch support is included and free. Search EffePadelle on the App Store.

A company day, a club afternoon, a birthday for thirty. The padel is the easy part.

Making it feel organised is what people remember. A screen on the wall does most of that: it shows everyone the thing is being kept properly, and it gives the people who are resting somewhere to look.

It works for a competition that runs all winter too. Leave the table up on the clubhouse screen and the group sees it every time they walk past.

EffePadelle. Mobile and desktop, free.

They booked the trip to Alicante in March and talked about it until June.

The best part of a padel trip is the week before it, so the chat opens before the competition does. Send the link and everyone's in, talking about that one weekend without scrolling past someone's holiday photos.

Then the weekend runs itself. Both mornings are a day tournament, the rounds are drawn for you, the timer calls the changes and the scores go straight in. The chat keeps the photos, and the argument about that one line call.

Swipe through it. One link opens the chat for your whole group. Free on iOS and Android.

posts.caption:
Every group has one who won't download anything.

They can play anyway. The host types their name on the invite screen and they're in the rounds, with partners, opponents, courts and a place in the table.

The catch: nothing gets kept for them. No profile, so their matches, points and ELO are gone when the competition ends, and no chat from their own phone. Usually around week two they see somebody else's profile.

Swipe for how it works. Bring them anyway. Guests play for free, and so does everyone with an account.

Friday Night League. Round two, Chen and Luca against Sven and Alex.

This is a competition from the inside. Your next match up top, who you play with and against, and the group chat and the spectator link one tap away.

EffePadelle. Free on the App Store and Google Play.

Now every match counts towards your own profile. Your rating moves with every result, and you see the highest it's been, your rank among all players and your win streak.

The same profile carries over to every competition and tournament you join, so the trip in April still counts in November.

Swipe to see your record. Free on iOS and Android.

Competitive padel with the people you actually like. Free on iOS and Android.

This is all three in one. The next three days, one each: the police officers, the gardener and the terrace.

The first of three films from our fictional AI campaign. We wrote the script the way we'd write one for a shoot. Every frame after that was made with AI.

That doesn't mean you type a sentence and this comes out. You need to know what you're after and how to ask for it, and then you still throw most of it away.

Bingo is about the most recognisable game of luck there is, so the last scene went there.
